title: Use federated identity with a third-party service
summary: Federation lets separate security domains rely on agreed identity assertions or tokens, reducing duplicated accounts while introducing trust, availability, privacy, configuration, and vendor-governance responsibilities.
outcome: Given an on-premises, cloud, or hybrid integration, identify the federation roles, trust artifacts, protocol purpose, assurance boundaries, and controls needed before accepting a third-party assertion.
managerMindset: Federation changes where identity evidence is produced, not who remains accountable for access decisions, data protection, availability, and deprovisioning.

sections.title: Make the trust relationship explicit
sections.body: In a federated flow, an identity provider authenticates a subject and issues an assertion or token; a relying party or service provider consumes it to establish a local session and make an authorization decision. A client or principal may initiate the request, while the organization defines which attributes, audiences, issuers, signing keys, time bounds, and assurance claims it will trust. On-premises, cloud, and hybrid deployment change operational ownership and failure modes, but they do not remove the need for validation and local policy.
keyPoints: The issuer of an assertion is not automatically the owner of the resource being accessed.
Audience, issuer, signature, freshness, nonce or replay controls, and required claims are trust-boundary checks.
Federation delegates authentication evidence, not organizational due care or authorization accountability.

sections.title: Match protocol purpose to the integration
sections.body: SAML and OpenID Connect commonly carry authentication assertions for single sign-on; OAuth is an authorization delegation framework for scoped access to an HTTP service and is not, by itself, an authentication protocol. Federation design should document the trust agreement, metadata or discovery process, key rotation, attribute minimization, logout and revocation behavior, incident contacts, service levels, and what happens when the provider is unavailable or compromised. A third-party identity service can simplify operations while concentrating identity risk.
keyPoints: Do not describe OAuth access tokens as proof of user authentication without an appropriate identity layer.
Cloud and hybrid federation require vendor assessment, contractual controls, and tested failure handling.
Attribute release should be limited to what the relying service needs for its policy decision.

sections.title: Adapt federation trust to on-premises, cloud, and hybrid boundaries
sections.body: On-premises federation often connects local directories and applications under enterprise-operated network and certificate boundaries. Cloud federation adds provider tenancy, external endpoints, shared-responsibility configuration, and contractual availability or logging dependencies. Hybrid federation bridges both and must handle identity source, synchronization, trust direction, assertion claims, credential lifecycle, network reachability, deprovisioning, and failure behavior. In every location, validate issuer, audience, recipient, time, signatures, protocol state, and authorization mapping; configure least-privilege claims rather than trusting a successful login as complete authorization. Failure modes include overbroad cloud claims, mismatched identities, stale synchronization, unsafe local fallback, and a compromised identity provider issuing trusted assertions.
keyPoints: Make access decisions attributable to a subject, asset, action, context, owner, policy, enforcement point, and revocation path.
Test both expected allow behavior and abuse, failure, stale-access, or unavailable-dependency behavior.

workedExamples.title: Federated access to a cloud maintenance portal
workedExamples.situation: An organization uses its workforce identity provider for a cloud vendor portal. The vendor asks for a broad directory group claim and wants OAuth scopes that include all project data.
workedExamples.reasoning: The organization should constrain the audience, claims, group mapping, token lifetime, scopes, and privileged role assignment. Verify signatures and issuer metadata, test replay and deprovisioning, and contract for incident notification and availability. Use OIDC or SAML for the sign-in assertion and OAuth only for narrowly scoped API delegation when needed.

distinctions.difference: Federation establishes trust and assertion exchange between domains; SSO is the experience or session pattern that can be built on that trust.
SAML and OIDC can convey authentication and identity claims; OAuth delegates scoped resource access and does not by itself authenticate a person.
The IdP authenticates and issues evidence; the relying party consumes the evidence and still enforces local authorization policy.

misconceptions.misconception: A signed assertion means the relying party can accept every claim in it.
misconceptions.correction: The relying party must validate issuer, audience, signature, time, replay protections, claim semantics, and local policy before creating a session.

misconceptions.misconception: Outsourcing IAM transfers security accountability to the provider.
misconceptions.correction: The provider operates contracted controls, but the organization retains due care, risk, authorization, and compliance responsibilities.

misconceptions.misconception: OAuth access tokens prove who authenticated the user.
misconceptions.correction: OAuth expresses delegated access; user authentication requires an appropriate identity protocol or separately verified context.

recallChecks.prompt: Who authenticates the subject and who authorizes the resource action in a federation?
recallChecks.answer: The identity provider supplies authentication evidence; the relying party or resource service evaluates local authorization.

recallChecks.prompt: What is the key purpose distinction between OIDC and OAuth?
recallChecks.answer: OIDC adds an identity and authentication layer; OAuth delegates scoped access to a resource service.

recallChecks.prompt: Name three assertion checks before a relying party trusts a token.
recallChecks.answer: Examples include issuer, audience, signature/key, expiry and not-before times, nonce/replay protection, required claims, and acceptable assurance.

scenarioSeeds.scenario: A vendor's IdP outage would block all administrator access to a critical cloud service.
scenarioSeeds.decision: Document resilient break-glass access, provider dependencies, notification and recovery commitments, and test the path without weakening normal federation controls.
scenarioSeeds.why: Federation adds an availability dependency as well as a trust dependency.

scenarioSeeds.scenario: A relying party receives a validly signed assertion with an audience for a different service.
scenarioSeeds.decision: Reject it and investigate configuration or substitution risk.
scenarioSeeds.why: Signature validity alone does not prove that this service was the intended recipient.

studyPlan.learn: Study IdP, relying party, service provider, assertion, trust validation, SAML, OIDC, OAuth, and on-prem/cloud/hybrid operating models.
studyPlan.connect: Connect federation to D5.2 identity assurance, D5.4 authorization, and D1 supplier governance.
studyPlan.apply: Review a cloud federation design and list its trust metadata, claims, key rotation, outage, revocation, and contractual controls.
studyPlan.revisit: Explain why a signed token can still be rejected and when OAuth should not be treated as authentication.

review.notes: Independent AI review only. Claim evidence, exact content fingerprints, scope checks, visual and memory-map assessments are recorded in knowledge/quality/. No human expert review or exam-readiness claim.

visualLearningContract.teachingQuestion: When may a relying party trust an external assertion/token?
visualLearningContract.misconception: A signed token is valid for every recipient/time.
visualLearningContract.formRationale: Aligned columns make concept meanings, decision criteria and failure consequences explicit and comparable.
visualLearningContract.focalInsight: Validate issuer, audience, subject, time, signature/key, nonce/state and authorization mapping.
visualLearningContract.intentionalOmissions: Do not equate OAuth authorization delegation with authentication.
visualLearningContract.retrievalPrompt: Token for App A reaches App B: which claim rejects it?
visualLearningContract.textFallback:
Federated Identity: external identity trust. Decision: choose trust boundary Failure/example: tenant confusion
Identity Provider: issuer/authenticator. Decision: protect issuance/key rollover Failure/example: compromised IdP
Relying Party: A service that relies on an external identity provider’s assertion to establish information about a subject.. Decision: Validate issuer, signature/key, audience, time and replay protections, then map the subject to local permissions. Failure/example: A validly signed token intended for another service is accepted without checking its audience.
Federated Assertion: signed/scoped claims. Decision: validate audience/time Failure/example: replay
Trust Validation: issuer/key/name/time checks. Decision: reject invalid claim Failure/example: stale signing key
SAML: XML assertion federation. Decision: validate audience/signature Failure/example: wrapping attack
OpenID Connect: OIDC identity layer. Decision: validate ID token/nonce Failure/example: token mix-up
Oauth: delegated authorization. Decision: validate scopes/redirect Failure/example: OAuth called authentication
Identity as a Service: provider-operated identity. Decision: assign customer/provider duties Failure/example: unreviewed SaaS config
